title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
keyIdea: A rotated sorted array goes up, drops once, then goes up again; the minimum is right after the drop. Compare arr[mid] with arr[e]: arr[mid] <= arr[e] means mid…e is sorted, so the minimum is at mid or to its left (e = mid). Otherwise the drop is right of mid (s = mid + 1). Stop when s == e.

approaches.name: Scan everything
approaches.idea: Look at every number and keep the smallest.
approaches.why: Correct, but the problem asks for O(log n).

approaches.name: Compare with the left end (l <= r, track ans)
approaches.idea: If nums[l] < nums[r] the range is sorted: take nums[l] and stop. Otherwise record nums[mid]; if nums[mid] >= nums[l] the left half is sorted, go right (l = mid + 1), else go left (r = mid − 1).
approaches.why: Halves the range each step. Needs the extra "already sorted?" check and an ans variable because mid is thrown away.

approaches.name: Compare with the right end (s < e)
approaches.idea: arr[mid] <= arr[e] → e = mid (mid might be the minimum, keep it). Else → s = mid + 1. When s == e, return arr[s].
approaches.why: Halves the range each step; no ans variable and no special case for an unrotated array.

quiz.q: arr[mid] <= arr[e]. What does that tell you?
options: mid … e is sorted, so the minimum is at mid or to its left
The minimum is to the right of mid

quiz.q: Why e = mid and not e = mid − 1?
options: mid itself could be the minimum, so it must stay in the range
Because the loop is s <= e

quiz.q: Why is the loop while (s < e) and not s <= e?
options: It stops with one element left, which is the answer; with s <= e and e = mid it could loop forever

quiz.q: Why compare with arr[e] instead of arr[s]?
options: arr[e] works even when the array isn't rotated; arr[s] needs an extra sorted check
